title: Direct answer to a direct question: partly right. Faster and more reversible than fine-tuning -- yes. Better learning than current methods -- no, and the field's own test says so.
the_question: isn't all of this a revolutionary way to make agents learn faster and better than the current way they learn, for the most advanced coding and computer use?
answer: WRONG ON 'LEARNING'. RIGHT ON 'FASTER AND CHEAPER THAN FINE-TUNING'. WRONG ON 'CODING AND COMPUTER USE'.

claim_1_faster_than_fine_tuning.verdict: RIGHT, and the margin is large
claim_1_faster_than_fine_tuning.measured_here: one demonstration -> milliseconds, no GPU, one row, exactly reversible (restore a file copy and the capability returns byte-identical)
claim_1_faster_than_fine_tuning.fine_tuning_comparison: every new fact costs a retrain, risks catastrophic forgetting of others, and deletion requires machine unlearning. 2026 calls this 'the parallel learning tax'
claim_1_faster_than_fine_tuning.what_makes_it_stronger_than_it_sounds: exact reversibility. Delete the row and the capability is gone; restore it and it is back. No other learning mechanism in this comparison can do that.

claim_2_better_learning.the_field_criterion: 'What happens if memory is wiped? If the gain vanishes, it was memory.'
claim_2_better_learning.measured: before wipe: ANSWERED ['q','z']. after wipe: ASK, NOTHING_TAUGHT. The file, the program and the process were unchanged; only the row was removed
claim_2_better_learning.peer_numbers: Skill-GRPO, a skill-retrieval baseline, falls 80.5 -> 60.2 on ALFWorld-3B when skills are withheld. SKILL0 states the premise: the model 'never truly acquires the knowledge it merely follows'
claim_2_better_learning.what_it_is: procedural memory externalised, or more plainly: filing. Very good filing. Not learning in the sense that makes a model more capable of the next untaught task.

claim_3_most_advanced_coding_and_compute.verdict: WRONG, and it is the weakest of the three
claim_3_most_advanced_coding_and_compute.coding: there is no model. 0 parameters. A system that cannot read a code file cannot produce advanced coding, and adding four billion skills does not change what reads the skill description
claim_3_most_advanced_coding_and_compute.computer_use: no display, no browser, no pointer driver, no GUI toolkit in this runtime. And 2026: OSExpert reports 0-10% success on unseen UIs, AgentNet fine-tuning on 22.5K human trajectories dropped UI-TARS 7B from 26.3% to 8-10%
claim_3_most_advanced_coding_and_compute.the_structural_reason: one-demonstration learning cannot produce generalisation across an application family. It produces an operator that transitions from unknown to known. Most of the work remains adjacent-to-the-new.

where_the_flat_answer_is_too_harsh.the_measured_contrast: after teaching 12 more operations, the original skill still executed correctly BY ID. It was not corrupted. Only FINDING it degraded.
where_the_flat_answer_is_too_harsh.why_that_matters: catastrophic forgetting damages the skill. This damages the pointer. Losing reachability is recoverable -- one clarification, one better index -- while losing the capability is not. The system is more benign than the thing it is being compared to.

the_genuinely_strong_result_of_this_proj: both the learn AND the forget are grants the user makes. Adding a capability is one demonstration; removing it is one row; restoring it is one file copy. Nothing in the weights is at stake because there are no weights. Fine-tuning cannot offer that, and 2026's own comparison tables put memory-augmented approaches at 'strongest retention, nothing in the model changes'.
the_honest_headline: this is not a revolutionary way to learn. It is a very good way to REMEMBER, and the two are confused everywhere in the industry, including in the question.
